title: HBO Max Gets International Rights To ‘Diabolical: The Epstein Files’

The streamer’s parent, Warner Bros. Discovery, has acquired international rights to the 90-minute doc, which comes from Australia’s ABC. HBO Max will begin rolling out the true crime program from September 3 across its international footprint, marking its debut in the UK, Italy (excl Italian-speaking Switzerland) and the Netherlands. Other territories where it will have an exclusive SVOD window are Spain, Portugal, Greece, Turkey, Iceland, Cyprus, Malta, Israel and Ukraine, along with the Baltic and CIS regions. It also examines the alleged missed opportunities and institutional failures across law enforcement, legal and social systems that allowed his criminal activity to continue largely unchecked for years. title: Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 2:13am PT Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 7 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 21 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 29 minutes ago See All Netflix The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected “Possible Love,” directed by Lee Chang-dong , as South Korea ‘s official entry for the international feature film category at the 2027 Academy Awards. “Possible Love” marks Lee’s first feature in eight years, following “Burning,” “Poetry” and “Secret Sunshine.” The film centers on two married couples whose lives intersect after a funeral: Mi-ok and her laid-off husband Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who live quietly with their young son Cheol, and Ye-ji, a filmmaker making a documentary about workers who lost their jobs, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). When Mi-ok agrees to be filmed by Ye-ji, the two women grow close, while Mi-ok finds herself unsettled by an attraction to Sang-woo. As the two couples’ worlds overlap, cracks begin to surface in both marriages. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller A 15-member selection committee, chaired by film critic Jung Sung-il, made the choice. Other committee members included Kang Myung-chan, Kim So-young, Kim Jae-joong, Kim Tae-sung, Kim Hyun-chul, Moon Young-hwa, Song Kyung-won, Won Dong-yeon, Yoo Hyun-taek, Yoon Sung-eun, Lee Han, Lim Dae-hyung, Jung Yi-jun and Cho Hwa-sung. Popular on Variety In its evaluation, the committee cited the film’s polished craftsmanship and the clarity of its directorial vision, pointing to the tone and mise-en-scène that sustain a sense of pressure throughout the story. The drama was described as prompting reflection on gentle forms of violence, incomplete freedom and the nature of true happiness, alongside a labor movement sequence that the committee said captured layered social undercurrents. The committee also highlighted the film’s humanism and delicate direction, its dense, multidimensional character relationships, and its meditation on love, desire and original sin. Members called it the culmination of Lee’s perspective and preoccupations as a filmmaker, praising what they described as nearly flawless performances from the four leads. The committee pointed to the international feature category’s track record of favoring auteur-driven dramas, noting that Lee’s 2018 film “Burning” became the first Korean title to advance to the Academy’s foreign language film shortlist. Members also flagged strong anticipation from North American press and said a Netflix awards team is preparing a campaign for the film that extends to a best picture push. The film’s world premiere will be at the Venice Film Festival and North American Premiere at the Toronto Film Festival. Under Academy international feature film category rules, “Possible Love” must complete its local theatrical release in South Korea by Sept. 30. The film will open in Korean theaters Sept. 23, followed by select theatrical releases in Australia Oct. 22 and in the U.S., Canada, U.K., Ireland and Japan Oct. 23, before streaming globally on Netflix starting Nov. 6. South Korea has submitted films in the category since 1962 without a nomination for decades, until Lee Chang-dong’s “Burning” became the first Korean film to make the shortlist in 2018. Bong Joon Ho’s “Parasite” then won the category and best picture in 2020 – the first non-English-language film to do so – and Park Chan-wook’s “Decision to Leave” (2022) and “No Other Choice” (2025) both reached the shortlist without landing a nomination. The 99th Academy Awards are scheduled for March 14, 2027. title: Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ As Oscars Best International Feature Contender
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Bitters End International Chief Sayaka Ito Talks Japan’s New Generation, Indie Spirit & Expanding Into Sales Prime Video To Adapt CJ ENM Reality Format ‘EXchange’ In Brazil As ‘Love Transit’ Lav Diaz’s Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ Boarded By Heretic For Sales View All August 25, 2026 2:12am Possible Love Netflix The Korean Film Council (KOFIC) has selected Lee Chang-dong ’s Possible Love as Korea’s official entry for the Best International Feature category of the Academy Awards. Netflix, which financed and has international rights to the film, recently confirmed it will receive an Oscar-qualifying theatrical release in Korea, U.S. and other select territories following its premiere at the Venice and Toronto film festivals. KOFIC’s selection committee praised the film for its “cinematic completeness, the clarity of the director’s message and its excellent mise-en-scene”, also mentioning the strength with which Lee has portrayed the multidimensional characters and their complex relationships. Related Stories Below The Line 2026-27 Awards Season Calendar: Oscars, Emmys, Grammys, Guilds & More News Oscars: Czech Republic Selects Documentary Feature 'If Pigeons Turned To Gold' For International Feature Film Race Lee’s first film in eight years, Possible Love follows two married couples – a laid-off worker and his wife, and a documentary filmmaker and her husband – whose paths cross when the filmmaker sets out to film them, bringing both marriages face to face with their different lives and hidden desires. Watch on Deadline Co-produced by Anonymous Content and Korea’s NOWFILM and Pinehouse Film, the film features a strong ensemble cast including Jeon Do-yeon, who previously worked with Lee on Secret Sunshine , Sul Kyung-gu, Zo In-sung and Cho Yeo-jeong. Lee’s 2018 Burning , which won the FIPRESCI Prize in Cannes, became the first Korean film shortlisted for an Oscar in the international feature category, although it did make the final nominations. Korea also selected Secret Sunshine in 2008 and his 2003 film Oasis , making Possible Love his fourth film to be represent the country at the Oscars . Possible Love is premiering in competition at this year’s Venice film festival and has also been selected for the Special Presentations section of Toronto. title: ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 2:00am PT ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 17 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 30 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 38 minutes ago See All Manuel Harlan “ Pride ,” the joy-filled British musical based on the true story of Lesbians and Gays Support the Miners (LGSM), will transfer to London’s Bridge Theatre from Nov. 12, following sold-out seasons at Cardiff’s Sherman Theatre and the National Theatre’s Dorfman space. The production will mark the inaugural show at the Bridge Theatre, a 900-seat venue on the Thames near Tower Bridge, under its new ownership by Trafalgar Entertainment. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller “Pride” reunites the creative team behind the acclaimed 2014 film of the same name: director Matthew Warchus (“Matilda the Musical”) and writer Stephen Beresford (“The Last of the Haussmans”), who wrote the musical’s book and lyrics. Set during the 1984 U.K. miners’ strike, the show follows 24-year-old activist Mark Ashton as he rallies LGSM to form an alliance with a striking mining community in South Wales. Popular on Variety The musical features an original score by Christopher Nightingale, Josh Cohen and DJ Walde, drawing on protest anthems, pop, rock, disco and the Welsh choral tradition. The transfer cast includes Samuel Barnett as Jonathan, Matthew Durkan as Mike, Gillian Elisa as Gwen, Chris Jenkins as Gethin, Darren Lawrence as Cliff, Kirsty Malpass as Hefina, Madeleine Morgan, Sarah Pugh as Siân, Caroline Sheen as Maureen, Courtney Stapleton as Steph and Matthew Woodyatt as Dai, with further casting to be announced. Speaking with Variety ahead of the transfer, Warchus says he always treats a remount as a chance to “get access to it again and make little fiddly improvements and changes.” He never approaches an opening night as a finished product, he says: “The opening night is a record, a document of where you got to in the amount of time you had and with the resources that you had.” The move to a bigger house, he says, will also change how the production’s comedy and sound design land. “The difference between 800 people laughing and 400 people laughing is more than double,” Warchus says. “I think the comedy will really benefit from more people watching.” He points to the show’s layered sound design – the birds of Wales, chapel bells, the chants of striking miners, the cheers of the Pits and Perverts benefit concert – as an element he expects to intensify rather than dilute in a larger room. “Sound design always works better in larger spaces,” he says. Warchus adds that the production’s essential character, built on simplicity rather than spectacle, will not change with the move. “It’s still going to be a story that’s got a handmade feel to it,” he says. “Very basic props, no glitzy automation or hydraulics or anything like that.” The “Pride” film bowed at Cannes – where it won the Queer Palm – and went on to be distributed globally. Beresford draws a parallel to audience reactions when the film was first released. “There were reports in cinemas all over the world that at the end of the screening people would applaud as though it were a stage production,” he says, adding that theater audiences have taken to hugging strangers and sharing tissues by the end of a performance. Asked whether the story, set 40 years ago, has taken on new relevance, Beresford points to a line from a review of the film that has stayed with him: “Prejudice cannot survive proximity.” He says the story’s emphasis on LGSM members physically showing up for a community unlike their own still resonates. “It’s the proximity that matters,” he says. Warchus recalls watching a performance alongside recently appointed U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham and noticing how the audience responded whenever the word “hope” appeared in the lyrics. “It was like a bell being rung,” he says. The stage adaptation followed two decades after Beresford first tried to get the story told on screen. “It took me 20 years to get the film made,” he says. “Nobody would touch it, the film, with a bargepole.” Warchus says the pair spent a couple of years weighing whether to attempt a musical version at all, wary of tampering with a project both are proud of. “You have a strong sense of why what kind of idiot messes with something,” he says. “But then, on the other hand, it’s quite painful if some other putz messes it up and you don’t get a chance to do it.” Warchus credits Beresford’s writing as the reason he has anything to direct in the first place. “I wouldn’t have known the story if Stephen hadn’t written it up and added his own angle to it,” he says. Beresford, in turn, says what drew him to Warchus was an aversion to visual spectacle for its own sake. “Directors who say, ‘I’m going to CGI this and the camera’s going to swing underwater and then it’s going to’ I just it’s white noise to me. I’m not really interested,” he says, adding that their work together on the film centered on character. “We talked about who they were and what they wanted and what they didn’t want,” he says. “And in making a musical – Matthew has made a lot of musicals – but he has a fantastic detailed eye. And I think we complement each other very well and have the same taste, largely,” Beresford adds. Asked how the show balances the AIDS crisis and the defeat of the strike against its comedy, Beresford says the two are inseparable. “One of the most subversive and powerful weapons at our disposal is humor and cheerfulness and the particular black humor that comes from living through adversity,” he says. He recalls a 2015 Pride march where Anne Scargill, then the wife of former National Union of Mineworkers president Arthur Scargill, approached him. “She said, ‘You’ve made the truest film about the miners’ strike that’s ever been made,'” Beresford says. “And I said, ‘Anne, we both know that is not true.’ And she said, ‘It is. Because it’s funny.'” On the decision to commission an original score rather than build the musical around existing songs, as the film’s beloved soundtrack had done, Warchus says jukebox musicals tend to interrupt their own storytelling. “The songs stop the story every single time they turn up, because they can’t carry the story,” he says. “A true musical is a completely different thing, and that’s what we wanted to do.” Designer Bunny Christie’s set, built around the idea of a touring production that has “come out the back of a minibus,” was a deliberate choice, according to Warchus, who says he grew up watching similar scratch-built touring shows in the 1980s. “That’s definitely in my blood,” he says, adding that the production also layers in “a rock-and-roll lighting rig” to give the show the feel of a live concert during its Pits and Perverts sequence. Warchus says he gave Christie a physical brief during an early workshop, taping off a square around a crowd of test performers to demonstrate how much stage space the show’s crowd scenes would require. “I need it to be this crowded when we’re doing the Pride march or an event happening,” he recalls telling her. “Therefore, I need the stage to be this small, this size.” Beresford and Warchus also address criticism that the musical understates the role of LGSM’s lesbian members, a group that in real life numbered around 40 to 50 people, some of whom broke away to found the support group Lesbians Against Pit Closures. Beresford says the real-life group had to be condensed for the stage, with composite characters like Reggie and Steph standing in for several real activists. Warchus says the show’s small ensemble size, which has to account for understudies across both the Welsh and LGSM characters, further limited how many roles could be written. “We worked out we could have seven people,” he says. Beresford notes the production made a point of casting an all-female band. “They’re the lesbian band,” he says. “They represent the lesbians.” Asked what Ashton, who died of an AIDS-related illness in 1987, might make of the musical, Beresford describes him as a natural showman. “He was a huge, huge theatric,” Beresford says. “He loved camp … his whole political process was about making things fabulous.” He adds that Ashton would likely have one specific complaint. “He would be frustrated that I do not have a song which literally is the entire Communist Manifesto set to music, perhaps to a samba beat,” Beresford says. Warchus says he expects Ashton’s reaction would mirror those of LGSM members who have already seen the show. “I hope that he would laugh uproariously, and I’m sure that he would cry,” he says. “Pride” previewed to sold-out houses at the Sherman Theatre before opening at the National Theatre’s Dorfman in June, where it runs through Sept. 12. The musical is produced by P&P Productions in association with the National Theatre, Pathé, Calamity Films and David Binder Productions. title: CGI Animated Movie ‘Juul,’ Featuring Lenny Henry, Joins Studio 100 Film’s Toronto Sales Slate (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 1:57am PT CGI Animated Movie ‘Juul,’ Featuring Lenny Henry, Joins Studio 100 Film’s Toronto Sales Slate (EXCLUSIVE) By Leo Barraclough Plus Icon Leo Barraclough International Features Editor LeoBarraclough Latest Venice-Bound ‘Meteorite,’ Debut Feature From Colombia’s Sebastián Múnera, Acquired by MoreThan Films (EXCLUSIVE) 2 days ago Seth Rogen, Colman Domingo, Danny Boyle Join Speakers Lineup at Toronto Market Summit 4 days ago The Freyas, a New Awards Ceremony Celebrating Nordic Film and TV Talent, to Launch in Helsinki (EXCLUSIVE) 5 days ago See All Courtesy of Fabrique Fantastique Studio 100 Film has added CGI animated feature “Juul” to its international sales slate and will introduce the project to buyers at the Toronto Film Festival . The English-language voice cast features Lenny Henry , while five-time Grammy Award-winners Michael League and Bob Lanzetti of Snarky Puppy contribute to the original score. The film is directed by Tom Van Gestel and written by An De Gruyter. “Juul” is in production and is scheduled for delivery in Q4 2026. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller Set in the 1950s, Juul follows 17-year-old circus acrobat Juul, whose life changes forever after a tragic accident leaves her in a coma and declared brain-dead. Facing financial ruin, her magician father takes a desperate and morally complicated decision: he steals her body from the hospital and presents her as a “living puppet” to revive the failing circus. But Juul is still conscious, trapped inside a body she no longer controls. As her anger and resistance grow, her body begins to transform into porcelain, becoming a powerful symbol of her silent rebellion and her fight to reclaim her own identity. Popular on Variety Van Gestel said, “‘Juul’ dares to go where most animated films don’t. It tackles a dark, raw and difficult subject, but does so by keeping every character deeply human. At its heart, ‘Juul’ is the story of a young girl who is constantly being pulled down by the world around her. Yet, no matter how hard she is pushed, she finds a way to fight back.” The film is produced by Fabrique Fantastique (Belgium) in co-production with M.A.R.K.13 (Germany), Keplerfilm (The Netherlands), Mr Miyagi (Spain) and Avalon Films (Ireland). Studio 100 Film handles worldwide sales, excluding Belgium, Germany, Spain and The Netherlands. Lorena Booth, senior manager sales and acquisitions at Studio 100 Film, said, “’Juul’ represents the kind of ambitious animated storytelling we are increasingly looking to bring to international audiences. title: Liza Soberano Joins Jury for Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary, Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 1:54am PT Liza Soberano Joins Jury for Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary, Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) By Nick Vivarelli Plus Icon Nick Vivarelli International Correspondent @NickVivarelli Latest Liza Soberano Joins Jury for Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary, Presented During Venice Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) 45 minutes ago Orlando Bloom to Be Honored During Venice Film Festival With Filming Italy Award 19 hours ago Fulvio Lucisano, Italian Producer of ‘Planet of the Vampires’ and ‘What Have You Done to Solange?,’ Dies at 98 7 days ago See All Courtesy TK Filipino-American star Liza Soberano has joined the jury for the Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary, which will be presented by Artemis Rising Foundation during the upcoming Venice Film Festival . The prize, founded by the Golden Globes and Artemis Rising Foundation with support from Think-Film Impact Production, honors a documentary feature film in the festival’s official selection — either in or out of competition — “that exemplifies the extraordinary power of documentary filmmaking to illuminate important social issues through compelling storytelling,” according to a statement. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller Soberano, who moved from California to the the Philippines as a child, built a stellar career there before crossing over to make her Hollywood debut in Focus Features’ “Lisa Frankenstein” in 2024. She has a lead voice role in DreamWorks Animation upcoming “Forgotten Island” that will be released in September. Along with her creative work, Soberano is an active ambassador for Save the Children Philippines as well as an advocate for women and children’s rights, protection of children from online sexual exploitation and mental health. Popular on Variety “I’ve always believed that film has the power to do more than entertain — it can challenge injustice, offer safety, inspire hope and remind us of our shared humanity,” Soberano said. “Documentary filmmaking is where some of the most courageous and unforgettable storytelling is happening today. I’m honored to serve on this jury, because celebrating documentary filmmakers isn’t only about recognizing extraordinary talent; it’s where the future of cinema is heading,” she added. The Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary Award’s full jury will comprise Golden Globes president Helen Hoehne; Oscar-winning producer and founder of Artemis Rising Foundation, Regina K. Scully; Oscar-winning producer and co-founder of Impact Partners, Geralyn White Dreyfous; and founder and CEO of Think-Film Impact Production, Danielle Turkov Wilson. The winner will receive a cash prize of $10,000 from Artemis Rising Foundation. The Golden Globes, Artemis Rising Foundation and Think-Film Impact Production first partnered to launch a documentary prize at the 2025 Cannes Film Festival and then expanded the partnership to Venice last year. “Documentaries have become some of the defining cinematic experiences of our time,” said Golden Globes president Hoehne, noting that in the Venice documentaries selection “we see creatives continuing to expand what the genre can do.” Regina K. Scully, founder of Artemis Rising Foundation, said: “We are thrilled to continue our partnership with the Golden Globes and the Venice Film Festival to celebrate cinematic excellence and see documentary storytelling receiving the prominence and recognition it has long earned.” Commented Venice artistic director Alberto Barbera: “Venice has always been a home for filmmakers who expand the possibilities of cinema, and documentary has become one of the defining creative forces in contemporary filmmaking.” “As this art form continues to grow in creative ambition and global reach, it is only natural that its place within the international awards landscape continues to evolve. We are proud to host and support the Golden Globes Impact Prize for Documentary; we welcome every initiative that elevates this [type of] work and reflects its growing importance within our industry’s highest honors.” The 83rd Venice Film Festival runs from Sept. 2 to 12. full_text: Aug 25, 2026 1:51am PT Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 10 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 23 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 31 minutes ago See All Warner Bros. Discovery Warner Bros. Discovery has acquired international distribution rights to “Diabolical: The Epstein Files” for HBO Max , with the documentary rolling out across international territories from Sept. 3, marking its premiere in the U.K., Italy and the Netherlands. The documentary, produced and distributed by Australian Broadcasting Corporation, charts Jeffrey Epstein ‘s ascent, his trafficking network and his ultimate collapse. Epstein was convicted of sex offenses and is accused of orchestrating a sustained abuse and trafficking scheme that preyed on underage girls for years. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller The film also scrutinizes the failures across policing, the courts and social institutions that critics say let his abuse persist largely undetected for so long. Popular on Variety Investigators, legal experts, journalists and others tied to the case contribute first-hand testimony throughout the documentary. title: John Gore Studios CEO Hilary Strong Steps Down
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Jesse Whittock Jesse Whittock International TV Co-Editor @WhittockTweets More Stories By Jesse Lux Angeles Studios Assembles Exec Team To Lead On Indie Pics Up To $20M Fremantle Global Formats Boss Vasha Wallace Exiting ‘Got Talent’ Firm After Two Decades Sky Arts Slates ‘The Handel Scandal’ & ‘Dangerous Debussy’ Docs View All August 25, 2026 1:42am John Gore andHilary Strong John Gore c/o John Gore Organization / John Gore Studios - photo by Sean Gleason Hilary Strong is stepping down from her CEO post at John Gore Studios. This comes as theater and screen producer John Gore moves to bring the UK company and its U.S. sister, The John Gore Organization , together under a single holding company. Gore himself will now lead both operations. Gore, who has won more 25 Tony Awards, is framing the restructure as allowing for both companies to better coordinate their respective film, TV and theatrical businesses under on strategic vision. As we revealed back in January 2025, Gore fulfilled a long-held ambition to launch a British studio, with veteran TV producer Hilary Strong taking on the CEO post to oversee a slate that included Joan Collins-starring Wallis Sampson biopic. No word on her next move, but she exits as a “friend and supporter of John Gore Studios as she explores exciting new opportunities,” according to the company. “I have adored my time working with John and the wonderful team we have put together to create John Gore Studios, and I will always be grateful to John for the opportunity, but we have both agreed that, with the reshaping of the global business, my work here is done. title: ‘Strictly Come Dancing’ Star Giovanni Pernice Felt Suicidal After Being Dropped By BBC Over Amanda Abbington Complaint: “They Hung Me Out To Dry”

In an interview with The Daily Telegraph , Pernice said he was left feeling suicidal after being “hung out to dry” by the BBC, arguing that the broadcaster’s duty of care did not extend to him. Pernice has not appeared on Strictly (the format on which Dancing with the Stars is based) since 2023, when he clashed with dance partner Abbington, who later filed a complaint. The BBC’s subsequent investigation partially upheld some of her concerns , though the corporation was never specific about the nature of the allegations it deemed credible. The BBC apologized to Abbington for her experience on Strictly , which remains one of the UK’s most-watched shows. “I feel they hung me out to dry to cover their backs. I was devastated by that,” Pernice said in an excerpt from his memoir, Gio: Taking the Lead , published by The Telegraph . It wasn’t even the financial [side]. It’s more, I have to do something. I always wanted to be something. “I was thinking, ‘There’s no place for me any more in this industry. So what’s the point?’ That’s when I thought, ‘Well, let’s end this. There’s no point. Let’s end it. I’m never going to have back what I had.’” On the BBC’s repsonse, he added: “They didn’t look after me. ‘Well, you’re not contracted with us, your contract finished in December.’ Yeah, but I’ve been with you for nine years, so you can look after me. If I’m sending an email saying that I’ve got myocarditis and depression, you can’t even reply to me and say, ‘Oh, sorry if you feel a bit down’?” The BBC has been approached for comment. title: ‘Cairo Conspiracy’s’ Tawfeek Barhom to Star in Les Valseurs’ ‘Borderline’ by Oscar-Nominated Yves Piat (EXCLUSIVE)
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 12:38am PT ‘Cairo Conspiracy’s’ Tawfeek Barhom to Star in Les Valseurs’ ‘Borderline’ by Oscar-Nominated Yves Piat (EXCLUSIVE) The drama-comedy, set to start filming in the spring 2027, will be pitched at Haugesund’s Nordic Co-Production Market By Annika Pham Plus Icon Annika Pham Latest ‘Game of Thrones’ Star Kristofer Hivju Turns to Rom-Com With ‘True Love’ by ‘Little Did I Know’s’ Martina Haag (EXCLUSIVE) 1 day ago Icelandic Producer Hlín Jóhannsdóttir Sets ‘Just a Kid’ With Alief Ahead of Haugesund and Reunites With ‘Driving Mum’ Team (EXCLUSIVE) 4 days ago Haugesund New Nordic Films Reveals Standout 36 Nordic Projects and 15 Fresh Pics Set to Woo 300 Industry Attendees 2 weeks ago See All Tawfeek Barhom Courtesy of Les Valseurs Palestinian actor Tawfeek Barhom , best known for Tarik Saleh’s Cannes winner “ Cairo Conspiracy ” in 2022 and Palme d’Or winner 2025 for his short film “ I’m Glad You’re Dead Now ,” is set to headline the French pic “Borderline” by first-timer Yves Piat. A very loose feature-length version of Piat’s Oscar-nominated live action short “ Nefta Football Club ,” “Borderline” (Sur la ligne”) reunites Piat with producer Damien Megherbi , co-founder of French outfit Les Valseurs with Justin Pechberty. Popular on Variety Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller Joining the cast are Samir Guesmi (“Ibrahim,” “A Prophet”) and Lyes Salem (“ Nefta Football Club ,” “The Man from Oran,” “Munich”). In the Arabic-speaking pic, Barhom stars as Hichem, a customs officer on the Algerian-Tunisian border, who tries to provide a decent life for his wife Leila and little daughter Zineb. Caught up in a corrupt system, his integrity is put to test when he meets Tesla, a music-loving donkey lost in the desert with headphones over his ears and bags full of cocaine on his back. “During my research, I often had in mind the actor who played the lead role in Matteo Garrone’s “Dogman.” When Tawfeek accepted the role, I knew I had found my ‘dogman’: with his accuracy, fragility, and determination, he will be the perfect anchor for this film, which features colorful characters struggling in the chaos of their world,“ said Piat in a statement. Speaking with Variety , ahead of the film’s pitch tomorrow at the Nordic Co-Production Market in Haugesund, Merghebi said “there’s something undeniably compelling about Tawfeek’s acting style. “The film which sits between the cinematic universes of Elia Suleiman and the Coen brothers, navigates between realism and absurdity. The character of Hichem is an upright and honest man, who encounters financial hurdles. When he finds the donkey carrying the cocaine, he is faced with a moral dilemma: should he sell it on the black market or turn it over to the authorities? Tawfik will be perfect to portray the character’s inner struggle. “ “He’s also very hard working,” the producer added. “We want the film to feel authentic, particularly regarding the Arabic language; Tawfeek speaks Palestinian Arabic, but he is capable of fully immersing himself in a role and honing the specific Arabic dialect required here.” Digging into “Borderline”’s narrative, Megherbi believes the overarching theme of borders both real and moral, should play strongly internationally. “Together with Yves and co-writer Alaa Eddine Aljem, our idea was to approach the concept of borders in a cinematic and metaphorical way,” he explained. “On one hand, you have the running theme of the moral boundary. Will Hichem stay clean, on the right track when he’s surrounded by people involved in illicit deal-making? “ “Then you have the setting on the Algerian-Tunisian border. There is something inherently absurd about the very notion of a border, especially in the middle of the Sahara,” Megherbi observed. “Borders are human inventions. In North Africa in particular, they’ve been drawn practically with a ruler by colonial powers, yet they have real consequences for people’s lives. In the film we take them very seriously, and challenge viewers to reflect on them. But their inherent absurdity is also what triggers the humour.” Spanish Co-production The project is being co-produced by Les Valseurs with Spain’s Sumendi and BTeam, partners to the French outlet on Diego Céspedes’ “ The Mysterious Gaze of the Flamingo ,” (Un Certain Regard top winner in 2025), with funding from Catalonia’s ICEC, France’s CNC, Region Nouvelle-Aquitaine and Pays de la Loire. At this week’s Haugesund New Nordic Films market, Megherbi is hoping to add Nordic co-producers, especially from Norway. “We’ve already co-produced “ Elephants in the Fog ” (this year’s Jury Prize winner at Cannes Un Certain Regard) with Storm Films in Norway. I believe the kind of deadpan, absurd humor tends to resonate well in Scandinavia. “Nordic people also know what it means to be tiny in front of a huge, indifferent landscape, even if the temperature is a little lower in comparison with the Sahara!” he quipped. Part of a delegation attending the French Focus in Haugesund , Megherbi will also bring to the Nordic Co-Production the animation project “All the Softness in the World,” feature debut of Turkish helmer Ayçe Kartal, multi-awarded for the short “Wicked Girl.” The sweeping story is set from the early 1950s in Turkey, through to the disco era in Paris. A boy raised as a girl in Turkey to protect him from a family vendetta, flees to Paris. There he resumes his life as a young man, and overcomes his trauma through creativity as he enters the real of Haute couture. “We’re in early stages of financing,” said Les Valseurs co-founder who is looking for equity and technical partners. title: Na Hong-Jin’s ‘Hope,’ Netflix’s ‘Dead-End Job’ and ‘Blue Road,’ Disney+’s ‘The Remarried Empress’ Among Selections as Busan Unveils Korean Cinema Today, On Screen Lineups
full_text: Aug 25, 2026 12:25am PT Na Hong-Jin’s ‘Hope,’ Netflix’s ‘Dead-End Job’ and ‘Blue Road,’ Disney+’s ‘The Remarried Empress’ Among Selections as Busan Unveils Korean Cinema Today, On Screen Lineups By Naman Ramachandran Plus Icon Naman Ramachandran Latest Oscars: South Korea Selects Lee Chang-dong’s ‘Possible Love’ for International Feature Race 28 minutes ago ‘Pride’ Musical to Transfer to Bridge Theatre From November; Director Says Bigger Venue Means the ‘Comedy Will Really Benefit From More People Watching’ 41 minutes ago Epstein Files Documentary ‘Diabolical’ Lands at HBO Max in International Deal 49 minutes ago See All ©2026 PLUS M ENTERTAINMENT, FORGED FILMS CO LTD, AND NA HONG-JIN The 31st Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) has unveiled its Korean Cinema Today and On Screen selections, with Na Hong-Jin ‘s “ Hope ” among a nine-film lineup spanning Panorama and Special Premiere. “Hope,” Na’s latest feature, drew global attention ahead of release on the strength of its large-scale production and a cast including Hwang Jung-min, Zo In-sung, Hoyeon, Taylor Russell, Cameron Britton, Alicia Vikander and Michael Fassbender. The film was selected in competition at this year’s Cannes Film Festival and will screen at BIFF as part of Korean Cinema Today – Panorama, which rounds out its six-title lineup with four world premieres. Related Stories 'Josephine' Trailer: Channing Tatum and Gemma Chan Star as Struggling Parents in Sundance Award-Winning Psychological Thriller Among the Panorama selections, “The World Before” marks director Yoon Dan-bi’s return to Busan with her second feature, following a 17-year-old girl navigating unfamiliar feelings across an island summer; the film will world premiere at the Toronto Film Festival before its Asian premiere in Busan. Yoon’s 2020 debut, “Moving On,” won four prizes at BIFF in 2019, including the Netpac Award. Veteran actor Kim Hye-ja returns to the screen for the first time in nine years in “Still Shining,” the latest from director Song Il-gon, whose credits include “Spider Forest” (2004), “The Magicians” (2006) and BIFF’s 2011 Opening Film “Always.” The Panorama slate also includes Hong Sung-min’s directorial debut “Sinner,” starring Jung Sung-il and Park Ji-hyun; Lee Yong-jae’s directorial debut “Ugly Duckling Ms. Maeng,” pairing Lee Sun-bin with veteran actor You Chea-myung; and Kim Joung-hoon’s ensemble mystery “Final Interview,” led by Cho Yi-hyun, Kim Jae-won, Shin Seung-ho, Kang You-seok, Kwak Dong-yeon and Bae Gang-hee. Popular on Variety BIFF’s Korean Cinema Today – Special Premiere section, dedicated to prominent contemporary Korean commercial films, will feature three world premieres. “Cattle Run,” from first-time feature director Kim Ji-hyun, teams Ryu Seung-ryong and Park Hae-jun as estranged brothers who unite to protect a newborn calf during a village crisis. “Sapiens,” the feature debut of Lee Hu-bin, casts Jung Sung-il and You Chea-myung as a suspect and attorney working through conflicting testimony in a kidnapping case. “The Sorry Generation,” from Kim Sung-yoon, whose “Fragment” won the CGV Award and the Chorokbaem Media Award at BIFF in 2024, follows a comic family clash between an exorcism and an ancestral spirit, led by Jung Jae-young and Lee Yi-kyung. BIFF’s On Screen section, launched in 2021 to give audiences an early theatrical look at the year’s most anticipated drama series, will present three selections this year, each screening a portion of its episode order. Netflix’s “Dead-End Job,” directed by Kim Da-min, whose “FAQ” won the Aurora Media Award at BIFF in 2023, stars Lee Jae-wook, Ko Min-si, Kim Min-ha and Lee Hee-jun in a mystery centered on a suspicious part-time job; four of its eight episodes will screen. Disney+’s “The Remarried Empress,” an adaptation already drawing attention for its cast, brings Shin Mina, Ju Jihoon, Lee Jongsuk and Lee Seyoung to a romantic fantasy directed by Cho Suwon, known for “I Can Hear Your Voice” (2013) and “Still 17” (2018); three of its 10 episodes will screen. Netflix’s “Blue Road,” from Han Jun-hee, whose “Coin Locker Girl” played Cannes’ Critics’ Week in 2015 and whose series “D.P.” won Best Drama at the 2022 Baeksang Arts Awards, stars Son Suk-ku, Nagayama Eita and Kim Shin-rok in a cross-border murder mystery, with three of its eight episodes screening. The 31st Busan International Film Festival will run Oct. 6-15, in and around the Busan Cinema Center, with the 21st Asian Contents & Film Market held Oct. 10-13. title: Bitters End International Chief Sayaka Ito Talks Japan’s New Generation, Indie Spirit & Expanding Into Sales
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Bitters End International Chief Sayaka Ito Talks Japan’s New Generation, Indie Spirit & Expanding Into Sales Prime Video To Adapt CJ ENM Reality Format ‘EXchange’ In Brazil As ‘Love Transit’ Lav Diaz’s Venice Title ‘Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors’ Boarded By Heretic For Sales View All August 25, 2026 12:05am All Of A Sudden CineFrance, Bitters End EXCLUSIVE : Amid the resurgence of Japanese cinema on the international festival circuit over the past few years, one resolutely indie banner, Bitters End , has been quietly growing its profile across production, distribution and international sales. Founded three decades ago by producer-distributor Yuji Sadai, the company is more of a highly-regarded veteran than a snappy startup, but has managed to stay at the forefront of bringing international arthouse cinema to Japanese audiences – as well as taking new and established Japanese filmmakers to the world. Related Stories News Cannes Heats Up As Ryusuke Hamaguchi's 'All Of A Sudden' Gets 11-Minute Standing Ovation Festivals 'All Of A Sudden' Review: Oscar Winner Ryusuke Hamaguchi's Humane 3-Hour-Plus Exploration Of French Health Care Too Often Feels Like A Lecture - Cannes Film Festival The company had two films in Cannes official selection this year – Ryusuke Hamaguchi ’s competition title All Of A Sudden , which it co-produced and split sales duties with Cinefrance Studios, and Yukiko Sode’s Un Certain Regard title All The Lovers In The Night , which it both produced and sold. All Of A Sudden , which was Hamaguchi’s first film made in France, extends a long association between Bitters End and the filmmaker stretching back to his early Cannes title Asako I & II, and his Best International Feature Oscar winner Drive My Car . Watch on Deadline In addition, as the company expands its international sales activities under Head of International Business, Sayaka Ito, it has also picked up In My Father’s Room , the directing debut of celebrated writer Maha Harada, which has been selected for main competition at the upcoming San Sebastian International Film Festival. In My Father’s Room Speaking to Deadline on Zoom from Tokyo, Ito describes the expansion into sales as a “natural and organic move” for the company, “as we were already involved in the life cycle of a film, from production and financing to domestic distribution and marketing.” She adds that there’s also a solid business motivation behind the move as Japan’s arthouse market has “become increasingly challenging, making it more difficult to recoup production costs through the domestic market alone”. Of course, this is an experience shared by many Japanese specialist producers and distributors. Japan may be one of the few international territories to recover to pre-pandemic box office levels, but most of the spoils are going to local anime and franchise content, while the country’s storied arthouse cinema circuit, once the envy of the region, continues to contract. But at the same time, Japan is in the fortunate position of having a lot more to offer the international arthouse circuit these days. “We’ve seen a new generation of highly talented Japanese filmmakers emerging over the past few years, and we believe it’s important to ensure that their work reaches international audiences,” Ito says. Japan’s new generation has been one of the sensations of the festival circuit since it booted up again in real life following the pandemic. After years in which just a handful of established names – Hirokazu Kore-eda, Naomi Kawase, Takeshi Kitano and Kiyoshi Kurosawa – were appearing at major festivals, a host of new filmmakers have recently broken through. Cannes selected seven new Japanese films for last year’s edition, and around the same number this year, while other major festivals including Berlin, Locarno, Venice, Toronto and San Sebastian are also paying attention to Japanese cinema, with directors including Hamaguchi, Koji Fukada and Sho Miyake leading the charge. Sayaka Ito, Head of International Business, Bitters End Bitters End has been involved in many of these titles in different capacities – producing or taking part in the production committee behind the film; handling international sales for films it has produced, as well as third-party pick-ups; and also distributing films in Japan. In some cases, it handles Japanese distribution for films produced by other companies, with recent examples including Wim Wenders’ Perfect Days , Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s Wife Of A Spy and Neo Sora’s Happyend . Increasingly, the company takes on all three roles, as was the case with All The Lovers In The Nigh t and the three films it had playing in San Sebastian in 2025 – Miyake’s Two Seasons, Two Stranger s, which won Locarno’s Golden Leopard before playing in San Sebastian’s Zabaltegi-Tabakalera section; serial killer fable Sai: Disaster, co-directed by Yutaro Seki and Kentaro Hirase, which premiered in main competition; and Yukari Sakamoto’s White Flowers And Fruits in New Directors. Ito explains the company is not completely new to international sales – as it has handled a few titles it also produced over the years, including Shinji Aoyama’s Helpless and Nobuhiro Yamashita’s cult classic rock film Linda Linda Linda – but expanded this activity when she rejoined the company after a brief hiatus with streamer U-Next in 2023. While acknowledging that it’s a tough time for the international arthouse market, Ito says the company has managed to leverage the relationships it has built with distributors, sellers, producers and festivals around the world over the past three decades, as well as to tap into the buzz around the Japanese new wave. “There’s now a growing number of people who are interested in Japanese cinema, so we’re seeing more representation at an international level of both new talent and auteurs. We’re also seeing more companies that don’t usually buy Japanese films reaching out to us, or at least being more open to acquiring Japanese titles. So we think that’s a good sign.” Among recent sales successes, Hamaguchi’s All Of A Sudde n was pretty much sold out worldwide by Cinefrance and Bitters End (which handled Asian territories) before it even played in Cannes. Sode’s All The Lovers In The Night , based on Mieko Kawakami’s novel about first love and false appearances, has so far been sold to 12 territories including Several Futures for the US and Ritual Films for Canada. “We believe Sode is also one of the most important filmmakers working in Japan today. With All The Lovers In The Night , we were able to combine her distinctive artistic voice with recognizable elements such as leading actors Yukino Kishii and Tadanobu Asano, and Kawakami’s novel,” Ito says. All The Lovers In The Night Two Seasons, Two Strangers has been sold to 15 territories, including Several Futures in the US. “Miyake had previously presented films at festivals including Berlin, but we felt that his international profile still did not fully reflect his importance as a filmmaker,” Ito says. “The Locarno win allowed his name and work to reach a much broader global audience.” Staying Indie In A Corporate World What’s also unusual about Bitters End is that the company has managed to retain its independent status over three decades, without accepting any major outside finance – no small feat in a market where smaller companies tend to get swallowed up by studios or slowly fade away. Sadai, who prefers to keep a low profile and let the films do the talking, founded the company in 1994 after working in curation and distribution, naming it after the 1972 Roxy Music song (with the name also encapsulating the spirit of striving to the “bitter end”). The company started out distributing international films in Japan – the Dardenne brothers say Sadai was the first buyer to pick up their films – and has since released around 300 titles, working with a ‘who’s who’ of international arthouse cinema, including Jia Zhangke, Bong Joon Ho, Fatih Akin, Nuri Bilge Ceylan, Bela Tarr, Otar Iosseliani, Roy Andersson, Gianfranco Rosi, Mikhael Hers and Alice Rohrwacher. Bong’s Oscar winner Parasite is the company’s biggest ever release, grossing more than $40M in early 2020. Ito says it could have gone even bigger if the pandemic hadn’t hit. The company also works with Universal Pictures on its more specialist titles, including Manchester By The Sea , Anora and Oppenheimer – with the latter film resulting in a relationship with director Christopher Nolan that extended to also releasing The Odyssey this year. Sadai stepped into co-producing and investing in both local and international films back in the ‘90s, at a time when few Japanese companies got involved in international co-production. In addition to working with Japanese filmmakers such as Shinji Aoyama, Nobuhiro Yamashita and Naomi Kawase, he also co-produced the early titles of filmmakers including China’s Jia Zhangke, Iran-born filmmaker Amir Naderi and Kyrgyz director Aktan Arym Kubat. Bitters End was also a co-producer on anthology film Tokyo! , with sections directed by Bong, Leos Carax and Michel Gondry. Ito describes Bitters End’s taste as “director rather than genre-driven” and explains that the company tends to work with the same filmmakers over many years, patiently introducing their body of work to Japanese audiences: “We place great importance on a filmmaker’s individual voice and consider artistic quality, social and cultural significance, and the commercial potential all at the same time. “We rarely select films because a particular genre or trend is currently popular. We don’t specialize in genre cinema, although we’re open to genre films when they have a strong and distinctive directorial vision. Many of the films we handle are human dramas. They may address social or political subjects, but they tend not to present their messages in an overly explicit or didactic way.” Those choices can be seen in the company’s current and upcoming release slate in Japan, which in addition to The Odyssey , All Of A Sudden and All The Lovers In The Night , also includes Fatih Akin’s Amrum , Gianfranco Rosi’s Below The Clouds and The World Of Love from Korean filmmaker Yoon Ga-eun. The company is also leaning into classics with current releases including 4K restorations of Ryusuke Hashiguchi’s All Around Us and Hush! Meanwhile, on the sales front, Ito is getting ready to launch In My Father’s Room at San Sebastian, a festival that has become an important launchpad for the company’s productions and acquisitions. Based on Harada’s short story An Unnecessary Man , the film revolves around a young woman working in a museum who is handed a key to a room she wasn’t aware of following her father’s death. While retracing the steps of a man mostly written off by society, she discovers his deep appreciation of art, antiques, poetry and Japanese tea ceremony. Yu Aoi ( Wife Of A Spy ), Issey Ogata ( Silence ), Eita Nagayama ( Monster ) and Eri Watanabe ( Shall We Dance? ) head the cast. “The film has strong authentic Japanese elements, but also features the paintings of Mark Rothko, so it combines Western and Japanese culture in a way that resonates visually and spiritually,” Ito says. “We feel it’s a perfect fit for European festival audiences.” Without giving too much away, Ito also shares that the company’s upcoming slate includes a film from an acclaimed French director shooting in Japan, as well as some features based on original stories from debut Japanese filmmakers. “We also have an international co-production project with Asian partners currently in development. We hope to support both established directors taking on new challenges, as well as talented emerging filmmakers,” Ito says. title: Meet Mestiza, the Female Duo From Spain Mixing Flamenco and Electronic Music
full_text: × Skip to main content By Georg Szalai Plus Icon Georg Szalai Global Business Editor View All August 25, 2026 12:01am Mestiza Courtesy of Mestiza Spanish DJs Belah Sánchez and Patricia “Pitty” Bernad had their own careers. But in 2021, they teamed up under the moniker Mestiza . Since then, the Spanish DJ and producer duo has been finding a growing fan base with its combination of electronic music with flamenco influences. “We are the culture of flamenco mixed with the hypnotic energy of electronic music, creating a bridge between the ancestral and the futuristic,” their website says. In December 2023, Mestiza released the debut album Quëreles via their independent label Sacro Music, which also reimagined flamenco traditions through a club lens. In 2025, Mestiza became the first female DJ duo to get a residency at the Hï Ibiza club on the Spanish island known as a destination for electronic music lovers. Related Stories Movies Dominic Monaghan to Join 'Lord of the Rings' 25th Anniversary Reunion With Elijah Wood, More at CCXP Business Guillermo del Toro, James Gunn Join Crunchyroll's Inaugural Anime Future Forum After playing Coachella earlier this year, this fall, the women behind Mestiza are bringing their high-energy act, as part of its Sacro event series, to New York, where they will rock the Brooklyn outdoor venue Creekside – Under The K Bridge, and London, where the duo will bring its sounds to the legendary Roundhouse in Camden on Oct. 30. THR , in an email Q&A, asked Mestiza about the duo’s history, music and aesthetics, their respect for flamenco, which comes from Andalusia in southern Spain, and what’s next for them, including a possible cinema project. How and when did you two decide to become a duo rather than continuing your solo work? PATRICIA “PITTY” BERNAD Before Mestiza, we had both been DJing individually for around 15 years, so we each had our own careers, experiences and musical identities. When we started working together, we quickly realized there was something much more powerful in what we could create together. We shared a similar vision of music, while bringing different personalities and influences to it. At some point, it stopped feeling like a collaboration and started feeling like a project with its own identity. That was really the beginning of Mestiza. Mestiza, courtesy of Jorge Foley Can you tell me why you chose the name Mestiza, which I hear means “mixed,” and what it symbolizes? And what does “Sacro” mean and why did you choose that name for your label and events? BELAH SÁNCHEZ Mestiza comes from the idea of mixture, which is really at the heart of everything we do. We bring together different worlds: electronic music and flamenco, tradition and modernity, our Spanish roots and a much more global sound. We liked that the name could represent all of that naturally. Sacro means “sacred” in Spanish. When we created it, we wanted it to feel like more than just another electronic music event. There is something almost ritualistic about people gathering around music, dancing together and sharing the same energy. Sacro was born from that idea and has gradually become its own universe. I love electronic music and have heard and enjoyed flamenco music. Why did you want to mix them? PITTY For us, it was never about mixing flamenco and electronic music simply because it was an interesting combination. Flamenco is part of the culture we grew up surrounded by, and electronic music is the language through which we express ourselves as artists. The interesting part for us is finding the point where those two worlds can coexist naturally. We have enormous respect for flamenco and everything it represents, so the intention has never been to disguise it or turn it into a trend. It is about taking elements from our roots and allowing them to have a conversation with contemporary electronic music. Maybe that is also why it can connect with people in completely different parts of the world, even if they haven’t grown up with flamenco. How excited are you for your upcoming London and New York performances and the venues you get to play at? BELAH We are incredibly excited about both shows. In London, we’ll be performing at the Roundhouse, the iconic venue in Camden where artists like Amy Winehouse, Adele and Lady Gaga have performed. Bringing Mestiza to a stage with so much history is very special for us. Mestiza, courtesy of Leshea Lewis In New York, we’ve played many times before, but this will be the first time we perform for such a large crowd at an outdoor venue, so it feels like a very important moment for us. What role do fashion and style play for Mestiza? It feels like you are an “experience” that goes beyond music? PITTY Fashion has always been another form of expression for us. We don’t really separate the music from the visual side of Mestiza – what we wear, the stage design, the lighting and the imagery are all part of the same identity. Music will always be at the center, but we love creating an entire world around it. How key is female representation and empowerment for you and your work? BELAH We are very proud of what we’ve achieved as two women in a scene that has historically been very male-dominated, but we also want our work to speak for itself. Femininity is an important part of our identity, and for us, empowerment means being ambitious, being in control of our project and embracing who we are. If that inspires other women to do the same, it’s something we’re very proud of. Mestiza at Coachella, courtesy of Mestiza Courtesy of Mestiza Your live shows have a reputation for being very visual. Why? And do you have any interest in making movies or series – or making music for them? PITTY We think very visually when we create. We’re inspired by cinema, fashion, architecture and Spanish iconography, so naturally those references become part of our shows. We both love cinema and the whole cinematic world. In fact, we’re currently involved in a project we can’t talk about yet, but there’s a possibility that Mestiza’s music might be making its way to the big screen very soon. Is there anything else you would like to share? BELAH Mestiza is still evolving. What started as a way of bringing our roots into electronic music has become a much bigger creative universe. We want to keep exploring that through our music, our shows and Sacro, while always staying connected to where we come from. We still feel there is so much we haven’t shown yet. THR

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Extend Battle Atop U.K. and Ireland Box Office as ‘Insidious’ Makes Strong Debut

title: Dominic Monaghan to Join ‘Lord of the Rings’ 25th Anniversary Reunion With Elijah Wood, More at CCXP
full_text: × Skip to main content By Ryan Gajewski Plus Icon Ryan Gajewski Senior Entertainment Reporter View All August 24, 2026 11:23pm Sean Astin (left), Elijah Wood, Dominic Monaghan and Billy Boyd in 'The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring.' Courtesy of Everett Collection Frodo and Merry are plotting new adventures to honor the 25th anniversary of the Lord of the Rings film franchise. Dominic Monaghan is the second confirmed guest for the forthcoming CCXP26 fan event that takes place later this year in São Paulo, Brazil , following the previous announcement that Elijah Wood , aka Frodo Baggins himself, will attend. With the theme of “Fellowship Forever,” this year’s CCXP is held Dec. 3-6, and its full lineup will be announced soon. Monaghan made his feature acting debut as Meriadoc “Merry” Brandybuck in The Lord of the Rings: The Fellowship of the Ring , which was released in theaters Dec. 19, 2001, and also starred Ian McKellen, Liv Tyler, Viggo Mortensen, Sean Astin, Cate Blanchett and Orlando Bloom. Based on the writing of J.R.R. Tolkien, the New Line movie was the first in director Peter Jackson ‘s trilogy that collectively surpassed $2.9 billion at the global box office and scored 17 Oscars. Related Stories Business Guillermo del Toro, James Gunn Join Crunchyroll's Inaugural Anime Future Forum Business Trump Trade War With Canada Puts Film, TV Spending Rules in Crosshairs “CCXP has a tradition of bringing together the iconic names who have shaped pop culture history, and Fellowship Forever is the celebration that The Lord of the Rings fans truly deserved. Having Merry alongside Frodo on the CCXP26 stage is one of those moments that captures the very essence of the festival — epic, in the most literal sense of the word,” says CCXP vp of content Roberto Fabri. Monaghan returns to CCXP after attending last year’s edition, where he participated in panels and met with fans for autographs and photos. Not only did the musician and his Grammy Award-winning band perform at the storied venue for the first time ever, but they did so with accompaniment from the Los Angeles Philharmonic. The news comes two months after the 20somethings romantic comedy ended its Season 1 run on the Disney streamer. It is the latest casualty in the YA arena at Hulu, which also recently passed on its pilots Buffy: New Sunnydale , Foster Dade and Don’t Get High. Related Stories Cancellations and Renewals 2026 TV Cancellations Photo Gallery: Series Ending This Year & Beyond Cancellations and Renewals 2026 TV Series Renewals Photo Gallery Not Suitable For Work ‘s cancellation leaves multiple storylines up in the air for the professionally driven — and romantically entangled — quintet at the center of it, AJ (Ella Hunt), Josh (Jack Martin), Abby (Avantika), Kel (Nicholas Duvernay) and Davis (Will Angus), as the two-episode finale ended on a big cliffhanger and a couple of smaller ones . By the end of the closer, all five characters found themselves in love triangles, (AJ, Josh & Davis), (Abby, Kel & Kel’s theater colleague), with Davis and AJ’s employment also in limbo after they stood up to their arrogant boss Bill (Jay Ellis). The Warner Bros. TV-produced ensemble comedy, whose original title Murray Hill was changed by Hulu, was not a breakout but had done respectable business attracting viewers and creating buzz, leaving series creator/executive producer Kaling hopeful about a renewal when Deadline spoke with her at the time of the finale. Watch on Deadline “Our writers room has been up for Season 2, which is wonderful,” she revealed in June . “Of course, the big question is whether we’ll get an official pickup for production, I keep my fingers crossed. I love the show so much, I’m so glad that it’s doing well. One of the things that has made me so happy is how much the cast loves the show, and the writing staff loves the show, and the way that the cast expresses their love through all the social content that they’ve been doing.” The cancellation of Not Suitable for Work raises questions about the viability of series that bet on largely unknown young actors and do not follow the conventional YA romantic tropes. While it drew mixed reactions from critics with 54% on Rotten Tomatoes, the comedy was another crowd pleaser from Kaling scoring 82% with viewers on the platform. Not Suitable For Work completed Kaling’s trilogy loosely based on her life, which started with Never Have I Ever , which chronicles the teen experience, continued through college with The Sex Lives Of College Girl s, and ended with post-college life in New York on NSFW . The main cast of Season 1 included Hunt, Avantika, Angus, Martin, Duvernay and Ellis. Kaling executive produced with Charlie Grandy, Howard Klein and Greg Mottola. title: Taylor Swift on Dealing With Public Perception and Deciding Not to Opt Out Before Her Career “Got Unmanageably Big”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Kirsten Chuba Plus Icon Kirsten Chuba Events Editor kirstenchuba Follow Sign Up View All August 24, 2026 5:30pm Taylor Swift attends the Songwriters Hall of Fame 55th annual Induction and Awards Gala on June 11 in New York City. Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images After a very busy summer that included being inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame , releasing an original song for Toy Story 5 and, of course, getting married , Taylor Swift made a stop at the Grammy Museum in Los Angeles for a wide-ranging conversation about her career. “The Icon Sessions with Taylor Swift: A 20-Year Retrospective” event, presented by the Recording Academy ‘s Songwriters & Composers Wing, took place earlier this month and was released online on Monday, featuring Swift sitting down with Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. Related Stories Music Meet Tuide, Your New Favorite Girl Group (Exclusive) Music Madonna Tops U.K. Dance Charts a Record Fifth Time in 15 Weeks Early on in the chat, Mason Jr. asked the superstar how she learned to trust her instincts when sharing her music with the public, as Swift explained, “I’m making music because I’m playing for the fans. I’m putting this out for people who care about it and who look to music as a way to cope with their life in the way that I did; I think that if you can actually go through all those checkpoints, you realize that putting out music you’ve made that you love so much is not the path to universal validation. If you’re still doing it, then you love it for the right reasons.” She added that dealing with the public perception and analysis of her lyrics “sometimes fuels [her songwriting]. Sometimes when people are mocking me, it’s really fun to mock them back. Sometimes I like to just use words that they have to look up in order to talk shit about.” Swift also acknowledged that she has several “coping mechanisms” that she’s used throughout the years, and “one of them is saying, ‘You chose this. You chose this every day. You could have opted out of this any day before it got unmanageably big,’ and I decided not to because I love it that much. And that’s just where it begins and where it ends. Everything that comes with this ultimately is worth it, as long as I get to still make music.” The discussion touched on a number of her albums, including her Reputation era, which she described as “a time in my life when — for the very first time, not the last — people had really actively tried to misunderstand me, just in general, and to misunderstand what I was trying to say and to purposely misinterpret it.” Reflecting now on the 2017 album, Swift said, “I’m very proud of it when I look back on it. I think the things that I look back on now is when I’ve gone through something that was sort of an attempt to drive me insane — when you when you don’t allow that to happen, and you use art and music as a way to like barrel roll out of that, those are the moments I’m the most proud of.” Elsewhere in the conversation, Swift explained how she’s “not a big mood board artist” and usually decides on the aesthetics of an album as the last piece. She explained that she identifies as a “confessional songwriter,” but “I think it’s important to specify that not all shocking revelations you make about yourself are deep. Like just saying something dramatic, shocking and wild doesn’t make it something that’s going to help people, resonate with people, be an important story that sits in people’s minds, hearts and souls.” “We have to be purposeful. You can’t just like scream something crazy and be like, ‘I’m a confessional songwriter,'” she continued. “Just for the same exact reason why details should not be strictly decorative. Like let’s not be haphazard with these things, let’s make them count.” Swift also touched on the process of her Taylor’s Version album re-records, saying, “At first, it’s like when the dog actually did eat your homework, and you’re like, ‘Now I have to redo it all?’ And then I have to go in to the teacher and be like, ‘The dog ate my homework.’ The public and the media — since it hadn’t really been done before in that way and I guess on like such a big scale and so loudly and obnoxiously — the public kind of did a little bit side-eye me the way that a teacher would if you did say the dog had eaten your homework. That was an interesting place to start from and I had to sort of get myself from the place of being like everyone says this isn’t going to work and everyone’s saying like nobody’s gonna want to hear my new take on the same work.” In closing, Swift gave an acknowledgement to her early days as a country star, noting, “I love my country roots more and more the further along this path I get. I want to honor them more and more, and I feel more and more tied and more loyal to them, the people that shaped who I am as an artist and as a writer. That all happened in Nashville.” She finished with some advice to young songwriters in the audience, telling them, “I hope that you will show up to work even when the idea fairy doesn’t. I hope that you will not be the person who shoots down everyone’s ideas in the room, but has not brought any of your own. I hope that you will remember the ‘yes, and’ of the improv session that is your recording sessions and that is life as well. And I hope you remember that in the music industry, as wild and ever-changing as it is, enthusiasm can protect you from anything. I would know.” THR

title: Field Of Vision Debuts Ukraine War-Themed ‘When It Started To Burn’ On Ukrainian Independence Day
full_text: Continue to Deadline SKIP AD You will be redirected back to your article in seconds Skip to main content By Matthew Carey Matthew Carey Documentary Editor, Awards @mattcarey More Stories By Matthew Six Finalists To Vie For 2026 Library of Congress Lavine/Ken Burns Prize for Film, With Winner To Receive $200,000 ‘Vultures’ Swoops To Top Award At Oscar-Qualifying HollyShorts Film Festival: Winners List HollyShorts Festival Set To Propel Documentary Jury Award Winner Into Oscar Race View All August 24, 2026 4:29pm 'When It Started to Burn' Field of Vision EXCLUSIVE: On the 35 th anniversary of Ukrainian Independence Day, Field of Vision is launching a new documentary on Ukraine’s valiant fight to maintain its freedom. When It Started to Burn debuted on the Field of Vision platform Monday, the third in a trilogy of short films from director Anders Hammer that examine “conflicts and civilian resilience across the globe.” His 2023 film The Takeover centered on the Taliban’s return to power in Afghanistan after the U.S. military withdrawal; Do Not Split , a chronicle of pro-democracy protests in Hong Kong, earned an Academy Award nomination in 2021. Related Stories Documentary Wendy Williams Docuseries Set At Peacock News WildBrain Buys Personality AI In Deal Worth Up To $70 Million We understand Hammer immediately traveled to Kyiv after Russia embarked on its “special military operation” in Ukraine (as Russian President Putin euphemistically put it) in February 2022. Four years’ worth of filming have gone into the making of When It Started to Burn . Watch on Deadline The documentary short “focuses on the civilians making great efforts to contribute to the resistance [against Russian aggression] in every possible way,” notes a synopsis. “As the fighting continues with no end in sight, the mental impact of war becomes clearer, and lives are changed forever. “Following the journey of Kseniia, a Kyiv local who sets up a volunteer center while her children seek refuge abroad, we witness as landscapes are rendered unrecognizable and neighborhoods are abandoned in the Ukrainian capital. Yet as years pass and the war rages on, Kseniia must choose between fleeing herself to reunite with family or staying behind to protect what’s left of what she once called home.” The film not only documents the brutality of war, but also “the kindness of humans finding solidarity in the face of extreme danger.” Ukrainian Independence Day marks the day in 1991 when Ukraine achieved its freedom from a collapsing Soviet Union. (Putin, in his attempt to capture Ukraine, appears intent on trying to reestablish Russian hegemony over not only Ukraine but potentially all Eastern Europe.) Filmmaker Anders Hammer in 2021 Francisco Seco-Pool/Getty Images Hammer’s additional credits include the documentary series Our Allies , set in Syria and Iraq, for Field of Vision. Escape from Syria: Rania’s Odyssey , published by The Guardian , won a Webby Award and a One World Media Award for Best Refugee Reporting in 2018; it has gained more than 10 million views and 100,000 shares on social media. In Hammer’s native Norway, he has directed nine documentaries for the Norwegian investigative journalism program NRK Brennpunkt. Field of Vision, founded in 2015, is a “filmmaker-driven non-profit organization that commissions and supports films, filmmakers, journalists and artists that use innovative and artistic ways to explore contemporary global issues through a cinematic lens, and push the boundaries of nonfiction storytelling.” Its impressive slate includes American Factory , winner of the 2020 Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature, and the Oscar-nominated features Soundtrack to a Coup d’État , Ascension , Strong Island , and Hale County This Morning, This Evening ; and the Oscar-nominated shorts A Night at the Garden , In the Absence , and Do Not Split .
